title: Anne Sullivan at the Water Pump
text:
Helen Keller lost her sight and hearing to an illness before she was two. By the age of six she was a wild, frustrated child in Tuscumbia, Alabama, who kicked, grabbed food from plates and threw tantrums her loving but helpless family could not control. In March 1887 a twenty year old teacher from the Perkins Institution in Boston, Anne Sullivan, herself partly blind, arrived to teach her.

Sullivan spelled words into Helen's hand with her fingers from the first day: d-o-l-l for a doll, c-a-k-e for cake. Helen copied the movements like a game but had no idea they were names. Sullivan insisted on table manners and fought long battles of will with her, but she never stopped spelling.

On April 5, 1887, Sullivan took Helen to the water pump in the garden. While one hand was under the cold stream, Sullivan spelled w-a-t-e-r into the other, again and again. Suddenly Helen stood still. In The Story of My Life she wrote that she knew then that the word meant the wonderful cool thing flowing over her hand. She touched the ground and demanded its name, then the pump, then her teacher. By evening she had learned many new words. Sullivan stayed at her side for almost fifty years.
lesson: Patience that keeps trying the same loving effort, day after day, can reach someone who seems unreachable. Breakthroughs often come after long stretches where nothing seems to work.
source: Helen Keller, The Story of My Life (1903), chapter 4, with Anne Sullivan's letters
